skills: Year 1
Inorganic and organic pharmacy on paper and at the bench (PHR 101, 102, 107 and their labs PHR 104, 105, 113): name, draw and test.
A lab notebook habit from PHR 104 onwards - raw readings in ink, with units, the same day.
Physiology and anatomy as a map of the body you can draw from memory (PHR 109, 111).
The first Oral Assessment (PHR 112) covers every first-year course: start a question bank in week one.
Year 2
Pharmacology begins (PHR 213, PHR 219): one drug card per prototype, revised on a schedule.
Analysis you can calculate (PHR 210, PHR 216): titrations, dilutions and percent of label claim, with units on every line.
Biostatistics with real data (PHR 211, PHR 217) - a spreadsheet you built, not a worked example copied.
Aseptic technique and media (PHR 203; PHR 116 from Year 1) until it is automatic.
Year 3
Medicinal chemistry structures drawn, not memorised as pictures (PHR 301, 311 and labs PHR 306, 317).
A batch record you wrote yourself for one dosage form (PHR 303, PHR 308), with in-process checks.
Dissolution and pharmacokinetic calculations end to end (PHR 304, 313 and labs PHR 309, 318).
Marketing and management vocabulary (PHR 305, PHR 314) - the half of the industry that is not the plant.
Year 4
Clinical and community pharmacy cases (PHR 405, PHR 412): a prescription reviewed in writing every week.
Regulatory files and GMP words you can use in an interview (PHR 413).
PHR 414 Thesis or Project: a supervisor, a question, a report and an oral presentation.
PHR 406 in-plant training: the Google Form at the start of the final semester, a CV, one to four weeks inside a company, a report.
dept.career_intro: A B.Pharm from BRACU is the entry ticket to the pharmaceutical industry, to hospitals and to research. The printed syllabus leans towards industry - technology, analysis, regulatory affairs, marketing and management all have their own courses - and PHR 406 puts every student inside a company before the degree ends. These are the common directions; none of them is a BRACU rule.
careers: Production and plant
Running and supervising the manufacture of dosage forms under GMP.
PHR 212, 303, 402 and their labs; PHR 312 Pharmaceutical Engineering; the PHR 406 report; GMP vocabulary (tool 7).
Quality control and quality assurance
Testing raw materials and products, keeping the documentation that proves it.
PHR 210, 310, 410 and the analysis labs; assay calculations laid out every time (tool 5); a clean lab notebook.
Product development and R&D
Formulating new products and improving old ones.
PHR 201, 304, 313, 403; a thesis or project (PHR 414) with real data; a record of every formulation you made.
Regulatory affairs
Preparing and defending the dossiers a product needs before it can be sold.
PHR 413, PHR 314; the dossier checklist (tool 7); careful writing.
Pharmaceutical marketing and management
Medical promotion, product management, sales and planning.
PHR 305, PHR 314, the Business and Economics Forum or BIZBEE; presentation practice.
Hospital and community pharmacy
Dispensing, counselling and medicines management close to patients.
PHR 405, PHR 412, PHR 411; drug cards with counselling points; the prescription-review card.
Research and higher study
A master's or PhD in pharmaceutical sciences, pharmacology, chemistry or public health.
CGPA, PHR 414 with a publishable result, PHR 211/217 statistics, two recommenders who know your bench work.
Cosmetics, biotechnology and food
Adjacent industries that hire pharmacists for formulation and quality.
PHR 404 and PHR 409 (cosmetology), PHR 403 (pharmaceutical biotechnology), PHR 110 and PHR 203 (microbiology).

Independent, unofficial study product. Not produced by, affiliated with or endorsed by BRAC University. Always confirm with the Office of the Registrar, your advisor and your department.

book.text: Read this first

This planner puts your whole B.Pharm degree in one place: every published course, the rules that move your CGPA, the dates that cost money, and a working page for every week of the semester - on your phone, offline, with the arithmetic done for you.
What you are holding

items: **Degree** - the Bachelor of Pharmacy (Hons.) as BRACU prints it: every course, its credits and its prerequisite. Pick a semester and a grade per course and the CGPA, the credit map, the Ready / Locked checks and your semester-by-semester plan follow.
**CGPA** - the grading scale, a quick semester GPA, what it takes to reach a target, a retake what-if on BRACU's own rule, and the CGPA lines that decide waivers and standing.
**Money** - this semester's bill at the published rates, the whole degree roughly, and the dates that cost money with a countdown you can send to your calendar.
**Semester** - deadlines and tasks, your routine with a clash check, and the working pages of a semester (set-up, course pages, check-ins, finals plan), one set per semester.
**Toolkit** - the tools this department's work actually needs, with logs and calculators that count and flag as you type.
**Rules** - BRACU's own grading, retake, probation, load, scholarship and fee rules, with the source named under each.
**More** - clubs and careers, the printable pages, an assignment cover page, the Excel version of the tracker, and your backup.

book.text: What it is not

items: It is **not an official BRACU document**. Nobody at the university wrote, checked or approved it.
It does **not replace your advisor**, your advising sheet or the student portal. Those decide what counts toward your degree.

It is **a snapshot**. Course lists, fees, CGPA lines and dates were read from BRACU's own web pages on 20 October 2026. Universities change these. When a notice and this planner disagree - cross the old line out here, and the notice wins.

book.text: Start in 15 minutes

items: On **Home**, type your name, the semester you were admitted in and the semester you are in now.
On **Degree**, pick the semester and the grade of every course you have passed. Your CGPA appears at once, and every course shows Ready, Locked or Open.
On **Money**, type this semester's fee and drop dates from the Registrar's calendar; they count down on Home.
On **Semester**, put your sections into the routine and your deadlines into the task list.
Open the **Toolkit** when the work starts: labs, projects, cases, the final-year runway.

book.text: Your data

Everything you type stays in this browser on this device - nothing is sent anywhere, there is no account and no internet is needed. That also means a cleared browser or a new phone starts empty. So, now and then, open **More** and tap **Save this planner with my data inside**: you get this same file back with everything you have typed written into it. Keep that copy - open it on a laptop, send it to a new phone, or hand it to next semester's you.

If a browser refuses to keep your data between visits (some phones open files in a way that forgets), Home tells you so and offers the same button. Your planner is then simply the latest copy you saved.

items: I have saved a copy with my data inside once, so I know where the button is.

book.text: My own roadmap

The department does not publish a semester-by-semester sequence as text, so this map is yours to build. Work in pencil: gateway courses first, every semester at or above the regular-student load, every prerequisite checked. Total the credits in each box and re-draw the map after every results day.
the Rules tab - Rules that move your CGPA and your money

Most students learn these rules by breaking one. Read them once now. Everything here is taken from BRAC University's published pages as they stood in October 2026; the source is named under each section.
The grading scale
BRAC University's undergraduate scale, in force since Fall 2020. Both A+ and A carry the full 4.0.
A+ to D- are passing grades. F is failing: it earns no credit and counts as zero in your GPA.
How your GPA and CGPA are worked out

Every course gives you **quality points = credits x grade point**. Add the quality points for a semester and divide by the credits you attempted for a letter grade: that is your semester GPA. Do the same across all semesters and you have your CGPA. The policy page prints the same formula: the sum of (grade points x credits) over the credits attempted.
Three things students get wrong

items: **An F stays in the sum until it is retaken.** It adds credits to the bottom of the fraction and nothing to the top.
**A D- passes, but it costs you.** A 3-credit D- is 2.1 quality points against 12.0 for an A - and a grade of B- or below is what the repeat rule exists for.
**W, I, P and AU never enter the GPA.** A W costs you the fee and the semester's work, not grade points.

book.text: Codes that are not letter grades

rows: Incomplete. Given for unavoidable circumstances when the course is otherwise done.
Sit the make-up examination when it is scheduled. The policy page says an I turns into an F if the make-up exam is missed.
Withdrawal. You left the course inside the withdrawal window printed on the Academic Dates page. No credit, not in GPA.
Use it on purpose: the window closes in the third week of classes, and there is no refund for a W.
Pass, on a pass/fail course. Counts toward graduation, not in GPA.
Pass/fail needs the instructor's approval and 12 credits of letter-graded courses in the same semester; at most 4 credits a semester and 16 in the degree.
Audit. You sat the course without credit.

book.text: Source: BRACU 'Policies and Procedures' page, bracu.ac.bd/academics/policies-and-procedures.
Retakes and repeats
BRACU uses two words. A **retake** is for a course you failed; a **repeat** is for a course you passed but want a better grade in.

rows: Up to twice. A third attempt only by exception of the Head of Department or the Dean.
Once, within two semesters of your first enrolment in the course.
The policy page says the best grade counts toward the CGPA.
The policy page says the latest grade counts toward the CGPA.

Anyone with an F. The separate retake-and-repeat page (for students enrolled from Summer 2019) adds: if you had a D or F in more than one subject that semester, only the F may be retaken, and only once.
Students with a grade of B- or below, says the retake-and-repeat page; it also caps a repeated or retaken course at B+.

book.text: the Toolkit tab - The B.Pharm toolkit

Pharmacy at BRACU is a bench course, a calculation course and a memory course at once, examined by 26 labs, four year-end orals and a company that watches you for a month. Eight tools, one for each way you are tested.
1. Eight semesters, four years: the shape of the load

The programme page prints eight semesters in four years, with yearly totals of **43, 44, 43 and 34 credits**, and the university's Policies page sets the Pharmacy load at **18 to 24 credits a semester**. That is five to eight courses every semester, most of them with a one-credit lab attached, so the plan that matters is not which electives to take - it is which semesters carry the most labs.

book.caption: My eight semesters (copy from your advising sheet; the page does not split the years into semesters)

book.text: The 24 credits of General Education and electives outside the major are spread over the first three years, but the page never says which goes where. The Residential Semester at Savar sits in your third semester for the General Education courses - plan that semester's PHR load with your advisor.
Every theory course and its lab
Almost every PHR theory course has a paired one-credit lab; the course descriptions say so course by course. Take them together - a lab without its theory is a semester of guessing.

PHR 207 and PHR 208 are in the credit list but not in the Second Year outline; PHR 305 Pharmaceutical Marketing is in the Third Year outline but has no credit printed anywhere, so the Core rows in the Degree tab add to 137 against the page's 140. Ask your advisor which is right for your batch; do not 'correct' the map yourself.
2. The lab loop and the 90% rule

Twenty-six of your courses are laboratories, and the university's attendance rule is **90% for laboratory sessions** (70% for classes). A lab course is won in the hours around it: the preparation before, the record the same evening, and the viva at the end.

rows: Read the experiment. Write the principle in two lines and the calculation you will need, with the units already in place. List the glassware, reagents and their hazards.
Record raw readings directly in the lab notebook, in ink, with units and the instrument's range. Note every deviation from the method - a changed volume, a late reading, a cloudy solution.
Finish the calculation and the result statement. Write what the result means and the one most likely source of error. Tick the attendance tally below.
Be able to state the principle, the job of each reagent, the acceptance limit and what you would do if the result failed.

book.text: 6. The year-end Oral Assessment

Four one-credit courses are oral examinations: **PHR 112** at the end of the first year, **PHR 215** the second, **PHR 315** the third and **PHR 415** the fourth. Each covers 'all the courses taken' in that year, and the page says PHR 415 spans the first to fourth year. The course descriptions say the aim is your understanding of the contents and your communication skills - so the preparation is a question bank per course, built from week one, and spoken answers rehearsed aloud.

rows: Everything from the first to the fourth year

book.text: Question bank

columns.h: Question I would ask if I were the examiner

book.text: The oral routine

items: Four weeks out: list every course of the year and the three topics each lecturer spent the longest on.
Three weeks out: write ten questions per course, in the words an examiner would use. Fill the bank above.
Two weeks out: answer them aloud to a classmate, two minutes each, no notes. Mark the ones you could not finish.
One week out: a mock oral with someone who asks follow-ups ('why?', 'what if the dose doubled?'). Fix the follow-ups, not the first answers.
The day: say the principle first, then the detail, then stop. 'I do not know, but I would check ...' beats a guess.

book.text: Mark the oral in this app as a one-credit course on its own row - it counts towards the CGPA like any other course.

book.text: 8. The final year: thesis or project, in-plant training

Two things close the degree. **PHR 414 Thesis or Project (2 credits)** is last-semester work under a faculty supervisor that ends with a report and an oral presentation. **PHR 406 Industrial Training** is non-credit, but the degree is not complete without its report: the School's Industrial Training Process document says you become eligible only after you 'complete all academic activities of your final semester', train for at least one and at most four weeks, and apply through a Google Form at the start of the final semester with your academic and personal details, contact details and an updated CV. The School issues forwarding letters to companies with the Office of Career Services and Alumni Relations; each company sets the schedule for its group, and you follow its rules, safety requirements and confidentiality policies.

rows: A research area, three papers read, a supervisor who agrees the question fits one semester. A draft CV for the training form.

Methods working, data recorded in a notebook, results repeated once. Forwarding letter received; the company's start date and reporting place confirmed.
PHR 414 report submitted and the oral presentation given. Oral Assessment IV (PHR 415) prepared alongside.
One to four weeks in the plant: a daily log, the departments seen, questions asked. Training report written and submitted the way the School asks.

book.text: Where this degree goes

A B.Pharm from BRACU is the entry ticket to the pharmaceutical industry, to hospitals and to research. The printed syllabus leans towards industry - technology, analysis, regulatory affairs, marketing and management all have their own courses - and PHR 406 puts every student inside a company before the degree ends. These are the common directions; none of them is a BRACU rule.

items: This is an independent, unofficial study product. It is not produced by, affiliated with, endorsed by or issued by BRAC University, and it does not use the university's logo, seal or colours.
It is a study aid, not academic advice. Programme structures, fees, scholarship rules and dates change; the Office of the Registrar, your department and your advisor are the authority.
Found something out of date? Cross it out, write in the new figure, and carry on. A planner that is corrected by hand is a planner that is being used.

sheets.name: Final Year
sheets.title: Final-year milestones (PHR 414 Thesis or Project, PHR 406 in-plant training)
sheets.blurb: Thesis/project and in-plant training milestones with countdowns and overdue flags.
sheets.intro: List every milestone of the thesis or project and the in-plant training with an owner and a due date; the flags show what is slipping.
example: Example: training Google Form submitted with CV (overwrite me)

sheets.name: Drug Cards
sheets.title: Drug card index and revision schedule
sheets.blurb: Which drug cards exist, how well you know them, and which are overdue for revision.
sheets.intro: One row per drug or drug class. Set your confidence from 1 to 5 and the date you last revised it; the sheet flags what to revise next (low confidence first, then anything older than three weeks).

columns.f: =IF({Drug / class}="","",IF({Card made?}<>"Yes","Make card",IF({Last revised}="","Revise now",IF(OR(AND(N({Confidence (1-5)})<=2,{Days since}>3),AND(N({Confidence (1-5)})=3,{Days since}>7),{Days since}>21),"Revise now","OK"))))

sheets.name: Lab Log
sheets.title: Laboratory log and attendance
sheets.blurb: Every experiment, its record deadline, its mark - and the sessions you have missed per lab course.
sheets.intro: One row per laboratory session across all 26 lab courses. Records still to submit and your running lab percentage show at the top; mark a missed session as 'Missed' so the summary can count them against the 90% rule.
example: Example: limit test for chloride (overwrite me)
Why is the standard prepared fresh?

sheets.name: Pharma Calc
sheets.title: Pharmaceutical calculations
sheets.blurb: Dilution, percent-of-label-claim, percent strength and dose-volume arithmetic.
sheets.intro: Type the blue cells; answers appear below. Three columns let you run three problems side by side. Column C holds example values - overwrite them. A checking aid for coursework, not a clinical tool.

sections.title: Dilute a stock (C1 x V1 = C2 x V2)

rows.label: Verdict
rows.note: compared with the limits you typed - take limits from the monograph your course uses

rows.label: Solute (g for w/v or w/w; mL for v/v)

sections.title: Volume of liquid for a stated dose

sheets.name: Training Log
sheets.title: In-plant training and industry visit log
sheets.blurb: Hours and lessons from the PHR 406 in-plant training and any industry visit.
sheets.intro: One row per day or visit. Total hours and the departments you have seen show at the top - use the last two columns to prepare interview answers and the training report.

sheets.name: Applications
sheets.title: Internship, job and scholarship applications
sheets.blurb: Every application, its deadline and its stage.
sheets.intro: One row per application. 'Days left' counts down only while the stage is 'To apply'.
